/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
p=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out=Path('tmp/pdfs'); out.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
print('PAGES',len(p.pages))
print('METADATA',p.metadata)
parts=[]
for i,page in enumerate(p.pages):
    txt=page.extract_text()
    parts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+txt)
    (out/f'page-{i+1:02}.txt').write_text(txt)
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(parts))
print('\\n'.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import math
for k in [2,3,4]:
    n=2**(2**k)
    old_w=1/n
    new_w=2/n
    old_tier=math.floor(math.log2(math.log2(1/old_w)))
    new_tier=math.floor(math.log2(math.log2(1/new_w)))
    expected_rotations=math.fsum(1/j for j in range(1,n+1))-1
    print({'n':n,'old_tier':old_tier,'new_tier':new_tier,'log2_weight_ratio':math.log2(new_w/old_w),'expected_rotations_for_smallest_key':round(expected_rotations,4)})
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem through a simple modification of a familiar data structure. The double-logarithmic tiers and harmonic ancestor-counting argument provide a clear core static result, with the usual additive constant in the depth bound.

The counterexamples to deterministic frequency priorities and single-logarithmic tiers help explain the design choices. The cross-entropy formulation also gives an interpretable way to relate prediction quality to an access-cost upper bound.

The locally changing working-set scores and their bounded total mass are useful observations for studying temporal locality. The experiments cover several distributions, multiple baselines, and ten independent trials.
weaknesses: Corollary 2.7's update bound is false for the stated priorities. Let n = 2^(2^k) and initially assign every key weight 1/n, producing a standard randomized treap. Doubling one key's weight moves it from tier k to tier k−1, making it the root. This requires Θ(log n) rotations in expectation, whereas the claimed O(|log₂(w′/w)|) bound is O(1). Appendix C.1 also claims that deleting and reinserting proves a difference-of-logarithms bound, although this argument only supplies a sum of depth bounds. These are substantive gaps in premises used by the dynamic analyses; the aggregate working-set guarantee needs a separate valid proof.

The B-tree depth argument has an independent problem. Appendix C.1 sums only nonnegative tiers, although weights greater than 1/B create negative tiers. Its construction keeps different tiers in separate blocks: weights 1/4, 1/16, 1/256, ..., B^(−1/2), placed consecutively in key order, can therefore create Θ(log log B) successive blocks, although the claimed depth of the last key is O(1). Remaining keys can have sufficiently small weights. The proof also assumes B = O(sqrt(C_t)) for each tier without establishing a lower bound on C_t. The depth and high-probability guarantees require additional construction and analysis.

Several robustness claims exceed their justification. The proof of Corollary C.6 effectively treats a lower bound on p_x as a lower bound on q_x; an absolute-error bound permits q_x to be arbitrarily close to zero. Consequently, C.6 and the corollaries derived from it are unsupported without an appropriate smoothing construction or another argument. Separately, the cross-entropy upper bound does not establish that actual additional cost is exactly m times KL divergence. Theorem D.2 similarly substitutes the actual ideal-prediction cost for an upper-bound expression without justification.

The closest classical alternative is insufficiently addressed. Weighted treaps with weight-biased random priorities already provide expected O(1 + log(W/w_x)) search depth, yielding static optimality for arbitrary frequencies and the corresponding cross-entropy bound. Composite tiering could still constitute a useful contribution, but the manuscript needs to explain and evaluate its advantages over weighted treaps, beyond its comparison with Lin et al.

The experimental results contain unresolved consistency issues. Under the stated uniform oracle, every key has the same tier, so the proposed treap has exactly the standard randomized-treap distribution; Figure 4 nevertheless reports a substantial systematic advantage. Figure 5 also shows prediction-independent baselines worsening with KL divergence, which requires clarification about whether the true workload changes. Section 5.1 alternately describes the horizontal axis as unique keys and accesses. These issues prevent confident interpretation of the reported improvements.

The empirical evaluation covers static synthetic frequency oracles, leaving the dynamic working-set behavior, update costs, and B-tree I/O benefits untested. Reproduction also requires clearer workload generation, comparison-counting conventions, and implementation details. Smaller, repairable issues include missing additive constants in depth and entropy bounds, an expectation-only proof for Lemma 2.2's high-probability statement, and reversed work/interval claims in Figure 7.
